title: Crew-hours rows as one table

blocks.text: A transmission operator (fictional) schedules line inspections week by week. Each task may start in some weeks, and needs a given number of crew-hours in each week of its work: a three-week inspection might need 5, 0 and 3 hours (the middle week waits for a permit). Each week has a crew capacity. The planners' data arrives as two DataFrames, and you are to build the capacity rows' coefficients as one table, the way lesson 11.1.2 builds the budget rows.

The model's capacity rows, with $`J`$ the tasks, $`S_j`$ the weeks task $`j`$ may start in, $`W`$ the planning weeks, $`h_{j,k}`$ the crew-hours task $`j`$ needs in its $`k`$-th week of work ($`k = 0`$ is its start week) and $`C_w`$ the capacity of week $`w`$:

Write `hours_entries(options, profile, weeks)` in `entries.py`. `options` has one row per variable $`y_{j,s}`$, with columns `task` and `start`; the variable's column number is its position in `options`: 0 for the first row, 1 for the next, and so on. `profile` has columns `task`, `k` and `hours`. `weeks` lists the planning weeks.

Return a DataFrame with columns `week`, `col` and `coef`, one row per nonzero coefficient of the $`\text{crew}_w`$ rows: the variable in column `col` carries `coef` hours in week `week`'s row. Leave out zero coefficients and weeks outside `weeks`, and sort the rows by week, then by column (the row-major order a `ModelProto` wants). Use joins and filters on whole columns; no loop over rows is needed. About eight lines.

from __future__ import annotations

import pandas as pd


def hours_entries(options: pd.DataFrame, profile: pd.DataFrame, weeks: list[int]) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """The nonzeros of the weekly crew-hours rows, one table row each: week, col, coef.

    `options` has one row per variable y[task, start], columns `task` and `start`; the variable's
    column number `col` is its position in `options`, counting from 0. `profile` has columns `task`,
    `k` and `hours`: the crew-hours a task needs in its k-th week of work (k = 0 is its start week).
    """
    cols = options[["task", "start"]].reset_index(drop=True)
    cols["col"] = cols.index
    terms = cols.merge(profile, on="task")
    terms["week"] = terms["start"] + terms["k"]
    terms = terms[terms["week"].isin(weeks) & (terms["hours"] != 0)]
    out = terms.sort_values(["week", "col"])[["week", "col", "hours"]].rename(columns={"hours": "coef"})
    out["coef"] = out["coef"].astype(float)
    return out.reset_index(drop=True)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    options = pd.DataFrame({"task": ["T1", "T1", "T2"], "start": [1, 2, 1]})
    profile = pd.DataFrame({"task": ["T1", "T1", "T2"], "k": [0, 1, 0], "hours": [5, 3, 4]})
    print(hours_entries(options, profile, [1, 2, 3]).to_string(index=False))

cases.says: each start variable gets the crew-hours of its k-th week of work in week start + k
the entries are sorted by week, then by column
work that falls after the last planning week gets no entry
a week of zero hours in a task's profile gets no entry
a variable's column is its position in the options table, even when that table's index has gaps

origin.section: Every Row Family Is a Table of (row, column, coefficient)

concepts: each family of rows is computed as a table of row, column and coefficient with joins and filters
the planning export is read as tables, and a packed cost profile becomes one row per year of work
